content: NET-EN (Norethisterone Enanthate) is administered intramuscularly and should only be given by a trained healthcare provider. Compared to DMPA (Depot Medroxyprogesterone Acetate), NET-EN has a lesser impact on bleeding patterns. Users of NET-EN typically experience fewer days of bleeding during the first six months and are less likely to have no monthly bleeding after one year of use compared to DMPA users. Some users of NET-EN report side effects such as weight gain, headaches, dizziness, abdominal bloating and discomfort, mood changes, reduced sexual drive, and potential physical changes like loss of bone density. However, NET-EN offers health benefits, including protection against pregnancy-related risks and iron-deficiency anemia. While NET-EN may share some health benefits with DMPA, only those supported by research evidence are listed. There are no known health risks associated with NET-EN. When discussing side effects, it is important to explain that irregular bleeding, prolonged bleeding, and frequent bleeding are common during the first few months of use. Over time, users may experience no monthly bleeding. Other side effects include weight gain (approximately 1–2 kg per year), headaches, dizziness, and other possible effects. In special cases, clinical judgment is required to determine if NET-EN is suitable for women with certain conditions. However, in situations where other methods are unavailable or unacceptable, a qualified provider may assess the woman’s condition and decide if NET-EN is appropriate, considering the severity of her condition and access to follow-up care. For continuing users, healthcare providers should inquire about the client’s satisfaction with the method, address any concerns about bleeding changes, and provide the injection (which can be given up to two weeks late). Progestogen-only pills (POPs), also known as minipills, contain low doses of a progestin hormone similar to natural progesterone. They do not contain estrogen, making them suitable for breastfeeding women and those who cannot use estrogen-containing methods. POPs primarily work by thickening cervical mucus to block sperm and disrupting the menstrual cycle to prevent ovulation. The effectiveness of POPs depends on consistent use. For breastfeeding women, the risk of pregnancy is about 1 in 100 during the first year of use. For non-breastfeeding women, the risk is higher, with about 7 pregnancies per 100 women during the first year. Fertility returns immediately after stopping POPs, but they do not protect against sexually transmitted infections (STIs). POPs are safe for nearly all women, including those who are breastfeeding, have anemia, or are living with HIV. Some users of POPs report changes in bleeding patterns, such as irregular or infrequent bleeding, prolonged bleeding, or no monthly bleeding. Other side effects may include headaches, dizziness, mood changes, breast tenderness, abdominal pain, and nausea. For non-breastfeeding women, enlarged ovarian follicles may occur. It is important to explain that side effects are not signs of illness and often subside within the first few months of use. Women should continue taking POPs even if side effects occur, as skipping pills increases the risk of pregnancy. In special cases, clinical judgment is needed to determine if POPs are appropriate for women with certain conditions, such as a history of breast cancer, severe liver disease, or systemic lupus erythematosus with positive antiphospholipid antibodies. Certain medications, such as barbiturates or rifampicin, can reduce the effectiveness of POPs, so a backup contraceptive method should be used. Combined oral contraceptives (COCs), commonly known as the pill, contain low doses of both progestin and estrogen hormones. They primarily work by preventing ovulation. COCs are highly effective when taken correctly, with less than 1 pregnancy per 100 women during the first year of perfect use. Fertility returns immediately after stopping COCs, but they do not protect against STIs. COCs are safe for most women, including those who are not breastfeeding, have anemia, or are living with HIV. Some users of COCs report changes in bleeding patterns, such as lighter or irregular bleeding, as well as side effects like headaches, nausea, breast tenderness, weight changes, and mood changes. Acne may improve or worsen but usually improves over time. Rare but serious risks include blood clots, stroke, and heart attack. COCs also offer health benefits, such as reducing the risk of endometrial and ovarian cancer, alleviating menstrual cramps, and improving symptoms of polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS) and endometriosis. Women taking certain medications, such as barbiturates or lamotrigine, may need to use a backup contraceptive method, as these medications can reduce the effectiveness of COCs. The combined contraceptive patch is a small, flexible square that releases progestin and estrogen hormones through the skin into the bloodstream. A new patch is applied weekly for three weeks, followed by a patch-free week during which monthly bleeding occurs. The patch is highly effective when used correctly, with less than 1 pregnancy per 100 women during the first year of perfect use. Fertility returns immediately after stopping the patch, but it does not protect against STIs. Some users of the patch report skin irritation, changes in bleeding patterns, headaches, nausea, vomiting, breast tenderness, abdominal pain, and flu-like symptoms. Long-term studies on the patch are limited, but its health benefits and risks are expected to be similar to those of COCs. The patch helps protect against pregnancy, endometrial and ovarian cancer, and pelvic inflammatory disease (PID). It also reduces menstrual cramps, bleeding problems, and symptoms of PCOS and endometriosis.
